F(ab')2 is bivalent and therefore CAN cross-link and agglutinate, but because pepsin degrades the Fc it can no longer bind C1q to activate complement. Misconception: believing the antigen-binding (Fab) arms rather than the Fc initiate the classical complement pathway.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: neither digest keeps all functions. Papain separates the arms into monovalent Fab fragments (losing agglutination) and also removes the Fc as a separate piece, while pepsin destroys the Fc entirely (losing complement activation). Misconception: assuming controlled proteolysis leaves every effector function intact.

subtopic: Vaccination principles: passive (immunoglobulin) versus active (toxoid) immunity in post-exposure prophylaxis
learningObjective: Distinguish the kinetics and memory outcomes of passive versus active immunisation and justify their combined use in post-exposure prophylaxis.
stem: A person with a deep, contaminated wound has never been vaccinated against tetanus. At a single emergency-department visit they are given both an injection of human anti-tetanus immunoglobulin (preformed antibodies directed against tetanus toxin) and the first dose of tetanus toxoid vaccine (an inactivated form of the toxin). Which statement best explains why both preparations are administered together?
choices: The immunoglobulin provides long-lasting protective memory, while the toxoid vaccine neutralises the circulating toxin within minutes.
Administering both is unnecessary, because the injected antibodies completely prevent any response to the toxoid.
The immunoglobulin neutralises toxin immediately but leaves no memory, whereas the toxoid induces a slower response that confers lasting immunity.
Both preparations act by stimulating the patient's own plasma cells to secrete anti-toxin antibody within a few hours.
The toxoid immediately neutralises any toxin already present, while the immunoglobulin generates memory B cells for future protection.
explanation: Passive immunisation supplies preformed antibody that neutralises toxin at once, but those antibodies are not made by the patient, decay over a few weeks, and leave no immunological memory. Active immunisation (the toxoid) engages the patient's own B and helper T cells: it takes roughly 1-2 weeks to generate protective antibody but establishes memory for durable protection. Because the toxin can act before active immunity develops, immediate passive protection is needed to cover that gap, while the vaccine provides lasting immunity for the future. Both roles are essential, so both are given.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: this reverses the roles. Passively transferred immunoglobulin gives immediate but temporary protection with no memory; it is the vaccine, not the immunoglobulin, that generates lasting memory. Misconception: confusing which intervention supplies immediate protection versus long-term memory.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: passively injected antibody may partially dampen the vaccine response but does not abolish it, and immediate protection is essential because active immunity is not yet present; the combination is standard practice, not redundant. Misconception: overstating passive-antibody interference as complete suppression of the vaccine.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: the immunoglobulin (passive immunity) neutralises toxin immediately but its antibodies decay within weeks and induce no memory, whereas the toxoid (active immunity) takes 1-2 weeks to produce antibody but establishes durable memory. The two therefore complement each other, covering both the immediate gap and future protection.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: passively transferred antibodies are already made and do not depend on the patient's plasma cells. The vaccine does engage the patient's B cells, but antibody production takes about 1-2 weeks, not hours. Misconception: assuming passive antibody works by triggering the patient's own antibody synthesis.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: this again swaps the roles. The preformed immunoglobulin, not the toxoid, provides immediate neutralisation, and memory is generated by the vaccine, not by passive antibody. Misconception: interchanging the immediate-protection and memory-generating functions.

subtopic: T-dependent antibody responses: the hapten-carrier effect and linked (cognate) recognition between B and helper T cells
learningObjective: Explain how a hapten-specific B cell obtains cognate help from carrier-specific helper T cells, and why physical linkage plus carrier-specific memory determines a strong secondary response.
stem: A mouse is immunised with a small, intrinsically non-immunogenic chemical group (hapten X) that has been covalently coupled to carrier protein P, and it mounts a strong IgG anti-X response. Several weeks later the mouse receives a single booster injection. Assuming the mouse has never encountered any carrier protein other than P, which booster preparation will elicit the strongest secondary (high-affinity IgG) anti-X antibody response?
choices: Hapten X covalently coupled to the original carrier protein P.
Carrier protein P administered on its own, without the hapten.
Free hapten X administered on its own.
A mixture of free hapten X and free carrier protein P that are not chemically linked to each other.
Hapten X covalently coupled to a novel carrier protein Q.
explanation: A hapten-specific B cell binds X through its B-cell receptor, internalises the whole hapten-carrier conjugate, processes the carrier protein, and presents carrier-derived peptides on MHC class II to a carrier-specific helper T cell. This 'linked recognition' means a strong T-dependent secondary anti-hapten response requires two things: (1) memory helper T cells specific for the SAME carrier the animal was primed with, and (2) physical linkage of hapten and carrier, so that the hapten-binding B cell is the very cell that presents the carrier peptide. Only X coupled to the original carrier P satisfies both conditions.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: the hapten-specific B cell binds and internalises X-P, processes carrier P, and presents P-derived peptides on MHC class II; memory helper T cells specific for P (generated during priming) deliver cognate help, driving a strong, high-affinity IgG anti-X secondary response.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: carrier P alone contains no hapten X, so the anti-X (hapten-specific) B cells are never engaged and no anti-X antibody is boosted. Misconception: thinking that restimulating carrier-specific T cells is sufficient even without the B-cell (hapten) epitope.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: a hapten alone is too small to be processed and presented as an MHC-associated peptide, so it cannot recruit helper-T-cell help; without T help there is no class-switched, high-affinity secondary response. Misconception: assuming a hapten that engages the B-cell receptor can by itself drive a full T-dependent response.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: linked (cognate) recognition requires the hapten and carrier to be physically joined, so that the SAME hapten-specific B cell internalises and presents the carrier peptide; when they are unlinked they are taken up by different cells and the anti-X B cell receives no carrier-specific T help. Misconception: treating simple co-administration as equivalent to covalent linkage.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: although the B cell could present peptides from carrier Q, the mouse has no memory helper T cells against the novel carrier Q, so only a slow, primary-strength response is possible - the classical carrier effect. Misconception: assuming any carrier works because the B cell still binds the hapten.

subtopic: Vaccination principles: herd-immunity threshold with imperfect vaccine efficacy
learningObjective: Compute the vaccination coverage required to reach the herd-immunity threshold from R0 and vaccine efficacy, and recognise the conditions under which it is unattainable.
stem: A viral disease has a basic reproduction number R0 = 4. The available vaccine is only 60% effective, meaning that 60% of vaccinated individuals become fully immune while the remaining 40% stay fully susceptible. Taking the herd-immunity threshold to be the immune fraction (1 - 1/R0), what proportion of the total population must be vaccinated to reach that threshold?
choices: The threshold cannot be reached even by vaccinating the entire population.
explanation: The herd-immunity threshold is 1 - 1/R0 = 1 - 1/4 = 0.75, i.e. 75% of the population must be immune. Vaccinating a fraction V of the population at 60% efficacy makes only 0.60 x V of the population immune. Setting 0.60 x V = 0.75 gives V = 0.75/0.60 = 1.25, i.e. 125% coverage would be required. Since coverage cannot exceed 100%, even vaccinating everyone immunises only 0.60 (60%) < 0.75, so the herd-immunity threshold is unattainable with this vaccine.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 75% is the threshold immune fraction, which would equal the required coverage only for a 100%-effective vaccine; with 60% efficacy, vaccinating 75% immunises just 0.60 x 0.75 = 0.45. Misconception: ignoring imperfect efficacy and equating coverage with the immune fraction.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 80% does not follow from the correct relation V = (1 - 1/R0)/efficacy = 0.75/0.60 = 1.25; it is simply a plausible-looking high number below the true requirement. Misconception: guessing a round 'high coverage' figure without applying vaccine efficacy.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: required coverage V = (1 - 1/R0)/efficacy = 0.75/0.60 = 1.25 (125%). Because even 100% coverage immunises only 0.60 of the population, which is below the 0.75 threshold, herd immunity cannot be achieved with this 60%-effective vaccine.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 60% is the vaccine's efficacy, not the required coverage; vaccinating 60% of people at 60% efficacy immunises only 0.60 x 0.60 = 0.36 of the population, far below the 0.75 threshold. Misconception: equating the required coverage with the vaccine efficacy.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 0.45 = 0.60 x 0.75 multiplies efficacy by the threshold, which has no valid meaning here; efficacy should divide the threshold, not multiply it. Misconception: combining the efficacy and threshold figures by multiplication.

subtopic: Monoclonal antibodies: hybridoma production and the logic of HAT (HGPRT-based) selection
learningObjective: Deduce why HAT medium selects only B-cell/myeloma hybrids by combining genetic complementation (HGPRT) with immortality, integrating nucleotide metabolism and immunology.
stem: In hybridoma technology, antibody-secreting B cells from an immunised mouse (which are HGPRT-positive but die within a few days in culture) are fused with myeloma cells (which are immortal in culture but HGPRT-deficient and secrete no useful antibody). The fusion mixture is then grown in HAT medium, in which aminopterin blocks the de novo synthesis of nucleotides, forcing every cell to rely on the salvage pathway - a pathway that requires the enzyme HGPRT. Which cells grow out of this selection, and why?
choices: The unfused B cells grow and divide indefinitely, because the HAT medium immortalises them.
Only the hybrids grow, because aminopterin selectively kills any cell that secretes antibody.
Only the B-cell x myeloma hybrids grow, because the B-cell genome supplies functional HGPRT for the salvage pathway while the myeloma partner supplies immortality.
All cell types survive in HAT medium, so monoclonality results solely from the later single-cell cloning step.
The unfused myeloma cells grow, because their immortality lets them overcome the aminopterin block.
explanation: HAT selection exploits genetic complementation. With de novo nucleotide synthesis blocked by aminopterin, a cell can survive only if it can use the salvage pathway, which requires HGPRT. Unfused myeloma cells are HGPRT-deficient, so they die despite being immortal. Unfused B cells have HGPRT but are mortal, so they die within days regardless. Only the hybrid combines both required properties - functional HGPRT from the B-cell nucleus (salvage competence) and immortality from the myeloma nucleus - so only hybrids proliferate. Screening and single-cell cloning of the surviving hybrids then yields a monoclonal antibody.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: HAT medium does not immortalise cells; unfused normal B cells remain mortal and die within a few days even though they possess HGPRT. Misconception: believing the selection medium itself confers immortality.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: aminopterin blocks nucleotide synthesis in every cell irrespective of antibody secretion; it does not target secreting cells, and hybrids survive because of HGPRT complementation, not because secretion is somehow spared. Misconception: attributing the selection to antibody secretion rather than to nucleotide metabolism.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: because aminopterin blocks de novo synthesis, survival depends on HGPRT-driven salvage; only the hybrid unites the B cell's functional HGPRT (making salvage possible) with the myeloma's immortality, so only hybrids can grow indefinitely in HAT.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: HAT actively kills both unfused parent populations - myeloma cells through HGPRT deficiency and B cells through mortality - so it is a genuine selection step, not a neutral medium that spares everything. Misconception: thinking HAT does not select and that cloning alone establishes the hybrid line.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: unfused myeloma cells are HGPRT-deficient, so with de novo synthesis blocked they cannot use the salvage pathway and die, even though they are immortal. Misconception: assuming immortality alone guarantees survival regardless of the metabolic block.

subtopic: Independent assortment: counting genetically distinct gametes (2^n)
learningObjective: Apply the 2^n rule to quantify the variation generated by independent assortment, distinguishing it from n, 2n and n!.
stem: An animal has a diploid chromosome number 2n = 8. Considering only the independent assortment of its chromosomes at meiosis (that is, ignoring crossing over and mutation), how many genetically different gametes, with respect to the maternal or paternal origin of each chromosome, can a single individual of this species produce?
explanation: At metaphase I each homologous pair orients independently, so each of the n pairs contributes an independent maternal-or-paternal choice and the number of chromosomally distinct gametes from independent assortment alone is 2^n. With 2n = 8, the haploid number is n = 4, giving 2^4 = 16. (Crossing over would increase the figure further, but the question deliberately restricts attention to independent assortment.) The key is that the exponent is the number of pairs n, and the operation is a power of 2, not 2n, n or n!.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 256 = 2^8 = 2^(2n) treats all eight chromosomes as independent two-state units. The two homologues of a pair are not independent (a gamete receives exactly one of each pair), so the exponent must be the number of pairs n = 4, giving 2^4 = 16.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 8 is the diploid number 2n. This confuses the number of chromosomes in a cell with the number of genetically distinct gamete types, which is 2^n.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 24 = 4! treats the four chromosomes as if arranged in ordered permutations. Assortment is an independent binary choice per pair, not an ordering, so the correct operation is 2^n, not n!.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: with 2n = 8 the haploid number is n = 4. Each homologous pair aligns independently at metaphase I, contributing an independent two-way (maternal/paternal) choice, so the number of distinct gametes from independent assortment alone is 2^n = 2^4 = 16.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 4 is the haploid number n itself. This stops at n instead of raising 2 to the power n; each of the n pairs adds an independent factor of 2, so the count is 2^n, not n.

topic: The cell cycle and its control
subtopic: G1/S arrest from a DNA-replication-initiation block and the resulting DNA content (C-value)
learningObjective: Predict the arrest point and DNA content of cells whose cell cycle is blocked, integrating S-phase timing with checkpoint location and C-values.
stem: A population of asynchronously dividing human cells is treated with a drug that prevents cells from initiating DNA replication, so that no cell can enter S phase; cells that are already beyond this point complete their current cycle normally. After the drug has acted for longer than one full cell-cycle length, at which point will essentially all of the cells be arrested, and what will their nuclear DNA content be relative to that of a normal G1 cell?
choices: In metaphase, with twice the DNA content of a G1 cell (4C).
At the G1/S boundary, with the same DNA content as a G1 cell (2C).
At the G1/S boundary, with half the DNA content of a G1 cell (1C).
At the G2/M checkpoint, with twice the DNA content of a G1 cell (4C).
Not accumulated at any single point, but spread across all phases with DNA contents from 2C to 4C.
explanation: DNA is duplicated only during S phase: a diploid, unreplicated G1 cell contains 2C, and a G2/M cell contains 4C. A drug that blocks initiation of replication allows each cell to finish its current cycle (dividing if it was already past S), but the progeny then halt at the G1/S boundary because they cannot start S. Since S phase is never carried out, the arrested cells keep the unreplicated 2C content of a G1 cell. This contrasts with a spindle poison, which arrests cells in mitosis at 4C.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: metaphase arrest with 4C is what a microtubule (spindle) poison produces via the spindle-assembly checkpoint, not a replication-initiation blocker; it also wrongly assumes the DNA has already been doubled.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: unable to initiate replication, every cell finishes its current cycle, divides if it was past S, and its progeny halt at the G1/S boundary. Because S phase is never performed, the DNA stays unreplicated at 2C — the same content as a normal G1 cell.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: the arrest point (G1/S) is right, but a diploid unreplicated somatic cell contains 2C, not 1C. 1C is the DNA content of a haploid gamete; equating 'unreplicated' with 'haploid' is the error.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: this assumes the cells still replicate their DNA (reaching 4C) and then stall at the G2/M checkpoint. The drug blocks entry into S, so DNA is never duplicated and 4C is never reached.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: a specific block synchronises the population by funnelling cells to one transition (here G1/S); it does not leave them distributed across all phases. This denies that a checkpoint block accumulates cells at a single point.

subtopic: Distinguishing mitotic metaphase, metaphase I and metaphase II by pairing, and predicting the following anaphase
learningObjective: Distinguish mitotic metaphase, metaphase I and metaphase II from chromosome arrangement and predict what separates at the following anaphase.
stem: In a diploid organism with 2n = 6, three cells (P, Q and R) are each observed at a stage in which replicated chromosomes are aligned on the equatorial plate. In cell P, six replicated chromosomes are aligned individually (single file). In cell Q, the chromosomes are aligned as three paired groups, each group consisting of two homologous replicated chromosomes. In cell R, three replicated chromosomes are aligned individually (single file). Which one of the following statements is correct?
choices: In all three cells the following anaphase separates sister chromatids, because anaphase always separates sister chromatids.
P is in meiosis I because it contains six chromosomes; at the following anaphase its homologous chromosomes will separate.
R is in mitosis; at the following anaphase its sister chromatids will separate to give two cells with six chromosomes each.
P is in mitosis and Q is in meiosis II; at the following anaphase both will separate sister chromatids.
Q is in meiosis I; at the following anaphase homologous chromosomes (not sister chromatids) will separate, producing two cells that each contain three replicated chromosomes.
explanation: Metaphase I is recognised by bivalents — paired homologous chromosomes — at the plate (cell Q). Anaphase I is reductional: whole homologues are pulled apart while sister chromatids stay joined, giving haploid cells whose chromosomes each still have two chromatids. Both mitotic metaphase (cell P) and metaphase II (cell R) show single chromosomes aligned individually, but a mitotic cell shows the diploid number (6) whereas a meiosis II cell shows the haploid number (3). Anaphase separates sister chromatids in mitosis and in meiosis II, but separates homologues in meiosis I.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: anaphase I of meiosis separates homologous chromosomes and keeps sister chromatids joined. 'Anaphase always separates sister chromatids' is a common misconception that ignores the reductional first meiotic division.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: cell P shows six chromosomes aligned individually, which is mitotic metaphase. Meiosis I is identified by bivalents, not merely by chromosome number; six single chromosomes at the plate is mitosis, whose anaphase separates sister chromatids.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: cell R has only three chromosomes aligned singly, so it is haploid — this is metaphase II, not mitosis. A mitotic cell of this organism would show six chromosomes, and no division of a three-chromosome cell could yield six-chromosome daughters.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: cell Q shows three bivalents (paired homologues), the hallmark of metaphase I, not meiosis II; and the claim that every anaphase separates sister chromatids fails for anaphase I, where homologues separate.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: three bivalents identify cell Q as metaphase I. Anaphase I is reductional — homologues are pulled apart while sister chromatids remain attached — producing two haploid cells, each with three still-replicated (two-chromatid) chromosomes.

subtopic: Mosaic aneuploidy arising from post-zygotic mitotic non-disjunction
learningObjective: Explain mosaic aneuploidy as the result of post-zygotic mitotic non-disjunction, distinguishing it from meiotic non-disjunction, chimaerism and translocation.
stem: A newborn is investigated because of features suggesting a chromosomal disorder. Karyotyping shows that some of the child's cells have a normal 46,XY complement, while others have 47,XY,+21 (an extra chromosome 21). Both parents have entirely normal karyotypes in every cell examined. Which of the following best explains the child's mixed (mosaic) karyotype?
choices: Crossing over between the two homologous chromosomes 21 during meiosis.
A non-disjunction event during meiosis in one parent, so that every cell of the embryo was initially trisomic (47 chromosomes).
Fusion, early in development, of two genetically distinct zygotes — one normal and one trisomic.

Non-disjunction of chromosome 21 during an early mitotic (post-zygotic) division of a chromosomally normal 46-chromosome zygote, producing a 47-chromosome cell line alongside the original 46-chromosome line.
A translocation of chromosome 21 onto another chromosome in only some of the embryo's cells.
explanation: If the whole individual were trisomic, the extra chromosome would have been present from the zygote onward, indicating a meiotic error. A mosaic — coexisting 46 and 47 cell lines — instead points to a post-zygotic event: mitotic non-disjunction of chromosome 21 in a normal 46-chromosome embryo produces a 47,+21 daughter cell (and a reciprocal 45,-21 cell that is usually lost), while the remaining cells stay 46. Their descendants form the two cell lines. This must be distinguished from chimaerism (two separate zygotes), translocation (no change in chromosome count) and crossing over (no change in chromosome count).

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: crossing over exchanges segments between homologues but never changes chromosome number, so it cannot create a 47-chromosome cell line.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: a meiotic non-disjunction in a parent would make the zygote, and hence every cell of the embryo, trisomic (47). It cannot generate a normal 46-chromosome cell line, so it cannot produce mosaicism.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: fusion of two separate zygotes describes chimaerism, which requires two fertilisation events; the scenario is a single conception. This confuses mosaicism (one zygote, mitotic error) with chimaerism (two zygotes).
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: a normal 46-chromosome zygote that undergoes non-disjunction of chromosome 21 during an early mitotic division yields a 47,+21 daughter (and a usually-lost 45,-21 daughter), while the remaining cells stay 46. This post-zygotic error produces the two coexisting cell lines (mosaicism).
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: a translocation of chromosome 21 onto another chromosome does not raise the chromosome count to 47. The trisomic line here has an extra whole chromosome, so a numerical (non-disjunction) error, not a translocation, is responsible.

subtopic: Robertsonian translocation and familial (translocation) Down syndrome — 46 chromosomes but trisomic dosage
learningObjective: Interpret how a Robertsonian translocation produces familial Down syndrome with 46 chromosomes but trisomic gene dosage.
stem: A phenotypically normal woman has 45 chromosomes in all her cells: she carries a Robertsonian translocation in which one of her chromosomes 21 is fused to one of her chromosomes 14, giving the karyotype 45,XX,der(14;21). Her husband has a normal 46,XY karyotype. Their first child has Down syndrome, and karyotyping of the affected child reveals a total of 46 chromosomes, including the mother's 14/21 translocation chromosome together with two free (structurally normal) chromosomes 21. Which of the following best accounts for the child being affected despite having 46 chromosomes?
choices: The translocation introduced a point mutation into the chromosome-21 genes, producing the Down syndrome phenotype.
Because the child has 46 chromosomes, the child cannot have Down syndrome and must instead be an unaffected balanced-translocation carrier like the mother.
A non-disjunction event during meiosis in the father produced a sperm carrying two copies of chromosome 21.

The child carries three doses of chromosome-21 material — a normal 21 from the father, a normal 21 from the mother, and a third copy on the mother's 14/21 translocation chromosome — even though the total chromosome count is 46.

The child inherited the translocation chromosome from the mother and a normal chromosome 21 from the father, giving only two doses of chromosome 21; the Down syndrome results from disruption of chromosome 14.
explanation: A Robertsonian translocation fuses two acrocentric chromosomes (here 14 and 21) into a single chromosome. A balanced carrier has only 45 chromosomes but a normal gene dosage and a normal phenotype. When the carrier forms gametes, the trivalent can segregate so that a gamete receives both the free chromosome 21 and the 14/21 fusion; fertilised by a normal 21-bearing sperm, this produces a child with three doses of chromosome-21 genes carried on only 46 chromosomes — translocation Down syndrome. The lesson is that chromosome number and gene dosage are not the same thing, and this mechanism underlies familial (heritable) Down syndrome, which carries a raised recurrence risk.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: Down syndrome is a gene-dosage (trisomy) effect, not the result of a point mutation. The translocation alters chromosome structure and dosage; it does not mutate individual chromosome-21 genes.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: a normal chromosome count (46) does not guarantee normal gene dosage. Translocation Down syndrome is precisely the case of 46 chromosomes but three doses of chromosome 21, so the child is affected rather than a balanced carrier.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: the father is chromosomally normal, and a simple paternal non-disjunction would give a 47-chromosome child. The extra chromosome-21 dosage here traces to the maternal translocation, which keeps the count at 46.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: the child received a normal 21 from the father plus, from the mother, a gamete carrying both her free chromosome 21 and her der(14;21) fusion. That gives three copies of chromosome-21 genes; because two of them lie on one fused chromosome, the total count is 46 yet the dosage is trisomic — translocation Down syndrome.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: two doses of chromosome 21 would be the normal amount, and Down syndrome is caused by excess chromosome-21 dosage, not by disruption of chromosome 14. The affected child in fact has three doses of chromosome 21.

subtopic: Autonomic control of the heart: tonic vagal tone at rest revealed by muscarinic blockade (atropine)
learningObjective: Deduce that the resting heart is under net tonic vagal (parasympathetic) inhibition by comparing the resting rate with the intrinsic denervated rate, and predict the effect of a muscarinic antagonist.
stem: A denervated (transplanted) human heart, which receives no autonomic innervation, beats at an intrinsic rate of about 100 beats per minute. A healthy resting adult, whose heart is normally innervated, has a heart rate of about 70 beats per minute. This resting adult is given a dose of atropine, a competitive antagonist at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. Which of the following best predicts the effect on the resting heart rate, together with the correct explanation?
choices: It is essentially unchanged, because at rest the autonomic supply to the sinoatrial node is silent.
It rises, because atropine acts as a direct agonist at the β1-adrenergic receptors of the sinoatrial node.
It falls, because atropine blocks the noradrenaline released by sympathetic nerves at the sinoatrial node.
It falls, because atropine prevents acetylcholine from carrying the signal across the sympathetic ganglia.
It rises towards about 100 beats per minute, because atropine removes the tonic parasympathetic (vagal) slowing of the sinoatrial node.
explanation: The key inference is that the normally innervated resting rate (70/min) lies well BELOW the intrinsic rate of a heart with no autonomic input (100/min). The only way innervation can make the rate lower than intrinsic is if there is a net tonic inhibitory (parasympathetic/vagal) influence on the sinoatrial node at rest, acting through acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors. Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist: it removes this vagal brake, so the rate climbs towards the unopposed intrinsic value of ~100/min. Atropine does not touch sympathetic (adrenergic) transmission and does not block nicotinic ganglionic transmission.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: because the resting rate (70) is far below the intrinsic denervated rate (100), the node must be under active tonic vagal tone at rest — the autonomic supply is not silent. Misconception: that there is no resting (tonic) autonomic tone.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: atropine is an antagonist, not an agonist, and it acts at muscarinic (not β1-adrenergic) receptors. Misconception: that any agent which speeds the heart must be stimulating sympathetic receptors.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: atropine is a muscarinic (parasympathetic) antagonist and has no direct action on sympathetic noradrenergic transmission at the node. Misconception: that atropine acts on the sympathetic branch.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: ganglionic transmission in both autonomic branches uses acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors, which a muscarinic blocker such as atropine does not affect. Misconception: that atropine blocks nicotinic ganglionic transmission.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: the resting rate below the intrinsic rate signals dominant tonic vagal inhibition through muscarinic receptors; blocking those receptors with atropine unmasks the intrinsic pacemaker rate, so the heart accelerates towards about 100 beats per minute.

subtopic: Saltatory conduction: quantifying the conduction-time cost of a short focal demyelinating lesion
learningObjective: Compute total axonal conduction time by splitting an axon into segments of different velocity and recognise that a short demyelinated patch can dominate the total time.
stem: A myelinated sensory axon has a total length of 1.00 m and normally conducts action potentials by saltatory conduction at a uniform speed of 50 m/s. A focal demyelinating lesion destroys the myelin over a 5.0 cm (0.050 m) length of this axon; within the lesion conduction becomes continuous and slows to 2.0 m/s, while the remainder of the axon is unaffected. Approximately how long does an action potential now take to travel the full 1.00 m, and how does this compare with the normal conduction time?
choices: 20 ms — essentially unchanged, because such a short demyelinated segment is negligible.
44 ms — more than double the normal 20 ms.
21 ms — the lesion adds only about 1 ms to the healthy conduction time.
45 ms — obtained by adding the lesion time to the time for the whole 1.00 m taken at 50 m/s.
25 ms — the slow lesion alone sets the conduction time.
explanation: Total conduction time is the sum of the times for each segment (time = distance ÷ velocity). The healthy portion is 1.00 − 0.050 = 0.95 m and takes 0.95/50 = 0.019 s = 19 ms. The 0.050 m demyelinated patch, conducting at 2.0 m/s, takes 0.050/2.0 = 0.025 s = 25 ms. Total = 19 + 25 = 44 ms, compared with the normal 1.00/50 = 20 ms. The striking teaching point is that a lesion only 5% of the length, but conducted 25 times more slowly, contributes more than the entire remaining healthy axon and more than doubles the conduction time.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: although the lesion is only 5% of the length, conducting it at 2 m/s (25× slower) takes 25 ms, which is longer than the whole healthy axon — the effect is far from negligible. Misconception: that conduction time depends on length while ignoring the local velocity.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: the intact 0.95 m takes 19 ms and the 0.050 m lesion takes 25 ms, giving 44 ms, which is more than twice the normal 20 ms; the tiny demyelinated patch dominates the total conduction time.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: this comes from a decimal-place slip, treating 0.050/2.0 as about 2 ms rather than 25 ms; the lesion actually adds 25 ms. Misconception/arithmetic error in the division.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: this double-counts the 5 cm patch by conducting the full 1.00 m at 50 m/s (= 20 ms) and then adding the 25 ms lesion time; the fast segment is only 0.95 m. Misconception: failing to subtract the lesion length from the fast-conducting path.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: this ignores the 19 ms required for the remaining 0.95 m of healthy axon. Misconception: that only the slowest segment contributes to total conduction time.

subtopic: Chemical synaptic transmission: distinguishing a presynaptic Ca2+-channel defect from a postsynaptic ACh-receptor defect at the neuromuscular junction
learningObjective: Integrate the role of presynaptic Ca2+ entry in transmitter release with postsynaptic receptor pharmacology to distinguish a presynaptic from a postsynaptic cause of neuromuscular weakness.
stem: Two patients have muscle weakness caused by faulty neuromuscular transmission. In patient X, autoantibodies block the voltage-gated Ca2+ channels of the presynaptic motor-nerve terminals. In patient Y, autoantibodies block and destroy the postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors of the muscle end-plate. In both patients the enzyme acetylcholinesterase is present and functional. Which one of the following statements is correct?
choices: In patient Y, raising the extracellular Ca2+ concentration would fully correct the weakness by boosting transmitter release.
In patient X, a brief burst of high-frequency stimulation raises Ca2+ in the nerve terminal and transiently increases acetylcholine release, temporarily improving strength.
In patient X, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor relieves the weakness by increasing the number of acetylcholine receptors on the muscle.
In both patients the quantity of acetylcholine released per nerve impulse is reduced below normal.
In patient Y, a burst of high-frequency nerve stimulation increases strength because each impulse then releases more acetylcholine.
explanation: Neurotransmitter release depends on Ca2+ entering the presynaptic terminal through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels to trigger vesicle fusion. In patient X (presynaptic defect) fewer Ca2+ channels means less ACh is released per impulse; however, during a high-frequency train, residual Ca2+ accumulates in the terminal (facilitation), transiently boosting release and improving strength. In patient Y the release machinery is normal but functional receptors are scarce, so the postsynaptic response is the bottleneck: sustained activity causes fatigue (weakness worsens), and acetylcholinesterase inhibitors help by prolonging the action of the ACh that is released — they do not create new receptors. Correctly matching each mechanism to its site is the crux.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: patient Y's defect is a loss of postsynaptic receptors, so releasing more transmitter cannot 'fully correct' the weakness once receptors are the limiting factor; enhancing release mainly helps the presynaptic disorder. Misconception: that any neuromuscular weakness can be overcome simply by releasing more transmitter.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: because Ca2+ entry triggers vesicle fusion, high-frequency firing lets residual Ca2+ accumulate in the terminal (facilitation), transiently raising acetylcholine release and improving strength — the hallmark of a presynaptic (X) lesion.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors raise and prolong acetylcholine in the cleft; they do not create new receptors, and they chiefly help the postsynaptic defect (Y), not the presynaptic release defect (X). Misconception: that AChE inhibitors up-regulate receptor number.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: only patient X releases less acetylcholine per impulse; in patient Y release is normal and the defect is a shortage of functional receptors. Misconception: conflating a presynaptic release defect with a postsynaptic receptor defect.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: this describes patient X (presynaptic). In patient Y the limited receptors are the bottleneck and sustained activity causes fatigue, so repetitive stimulation worsens rather than improves strength. Misconception: swapping the presynaptic and postsynaptic disorders.

subtopic: Reflex-arc localisation: Bell–Magendie law and lower- vs upper-motor-neuron signs from a ventral-root lesion
learningObjective: Localise a lesion in a spinal reflex arc by combining preserved sensation, absent reflex, and flaccid paralysis, applying the Bell–Magendie law and distinguishing lower- from upper-motor-neuron signs.
stem: A patient is examined after an injury to the nerve tissue supplying one leg. On the affected side: a pin-prick applied to the skin over the quadriceps is felt normally; the knee-jerk (patellar tendon) reflex cannot be elicited; the patient cannot voluntarily contract the quadriceps; and the muscle is flaccid with reduced tone. Which single lesion best accounts for ALL of these findings?
choices: Section of the ventral (anterior) nerve root carrying the motor fibres to the leg.
Section of the dorsal (posterior) nerve root carrying the sensory fibres from the leg.
A lesion of the dorsal columns of the spinal cord on that side.
A lesion of the corticospinal (upper motor neuron) tract in the spinal cord.
Section of a peripheral mixed nerve supplying the quadriceps.
explanation: By the Bell–Magendie law the dorsal root is sensory (afferent) and the ventral root is motor (efferent). Preserved pin-prick sensation rules out any lesion of the afferent limb or of a mixed nerve/tract that carries sensation. Absent reflex plus absent voluntary contraction plus flaccidity with reduced tone are the classic signs of a lower-motor-neuron (efferent) lesion. The only structure whose loss spares all sensation yet removes both the efferent limb of the stretch reflex and the sole motor pathway to the muscle is the ventral root. An upper-motor-neuron lesion would instead give increased tone and exaggerated reflexes, so it is excluded.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: the ventral root is the purely motor (efferent) limb; its section spares all sensory input (pin-prick intact) but removes the efferent limb of the stretch reflex (areflexia) and the only motor path to the muscle (no voluntary contraction, flaccidity, reduced tone) — the classic lower-motor-neuron picture and a direct application of the Bell–Magendie law.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: cutting the dorsal root would abolish cutaneous sensation from that region as well as the afferent limb of the reflex, but here pin-prick sensation is preserved. Misconception: assuming an absent reflex must arise from the sensory (afferent) limb.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: a dorsal-column lesion impairs fine touch and proprioception but leaves the local monosynaptic reflex and voluntary power essentially intact and cannot explain flaccid paralysis. Misconception: attributing motor and reflex loss to an ascending sensory pathway.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: an upper-motor-neuron (corticospinal) lesion causes weakness but with increased tone and exaggerated (hyperactive) reflexes, not an absent reflex with flaccidity, and sensation is spared. Misconception: confusing upper-motor-neuron with lower-motor-neuron signs.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: a mixed peripheral nerve carries both sensory and motor fibres, so its section would also abolish sensation, contradicting the preserved pin-prick. Misconception: not distinguishing a mixed nerve from a purely motor ventral root.

subtopic: Synaptic reversal potential of a channel permeable to both Na+ and K+ (the end-plate potential)
learningObjective: Calculate the reversal potential of a synaptic channel equally permeable to Na+ and K+ as the mean of the two equilibrium potentials, and explain why the end-plate depolarises towards this value rather than to either single-ion equilibrium potential.
stem: When acetylcholine opens the nicotinic receptor channel at a neuromuscular junction, the open channel is approximately equally permeable (equal conductance) to Na+ and to K+. For this muscle cell the equilibrium (Nernst) potential for Na+ is +60 mV and that for K+ is −90 mV; the resting membrane potential is −80 mV. If a large number of these channels are held open, the membrane potential of the end-plate is driven towards the value at which the net current through the channels is zero (the reversal potential of the end-plate current). Approximately which value is this?
choices: About −75 mV.
About −80 mV; opening the channels does not change the membrane potential.
About −90 mV, the K+ equilibrium potential.
About +60 mV, the Na+ equilibrium potential.
About −15 mV.
explanation: The net current carried by the open channels is I = g_Na(V − E_Na) + g_K(V − E_K). Because the channel is equally permeable to the two ions, g_Na = g_K = g, so the reversal potential (where I = 0) satisfies (V − E_Na) + (V − E_K) = 0, giving V = (E_Na + E_K)/2 = (+60 + (−90))/2 = −15 mV. The end-plate therefore depolarises from the resting −80 mV towards about −15 mV: a value that lies BETWEEN the two single-ion equilibrium potentials, because Na+ influx (which alone would drive V to +60 mV) is opposed by K+ efflux (which alone would drive V to −90 mV). At −80 mV the inward Na+ driving force (V − E_Na = −140 mV) hugely exceeds the small outward K+ driving force (V − E_K = +10 mV), so net current is inward and the membrane depolarises.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: −75 mV results from a sign error such as computing (−90 − 60)/2, i.e. giving the Na+ equilibrium potential the wrong sign; the correct mean is (+60 − 90)/2 = −15 mV. Misconception/arithmetic sign error.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: at −80 mV the large inward Na+ driving force (V − E_Na = −140 mV) greatly exceeds the small outward K+ driving force (V − E_K = +10 mV), so net current is inward and the membrane depolarises rather than staying at rest. Misconception: that opening ion channels leaves the membrane potential unchanged.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: −90 mV is the K+ equilibrium potential, but the channel is not K+-selective, and driving the membrane there would be hyperpolarising (inhibitory), the opposite of the observed depolarising end-plate potential. Misconception: assuming the channel behaves like a pure K+ channel.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: the channel is not Na+-selective, so it does not drive the membrane to E_Na; the simultaneous K+ efflux pulls the reversal potential far below +60 mV. Misconception: treating the excitatory channel as if it were selective for Na+ alone.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: with equal Na+ and K+ conductance, the net current g(V − E_Na) + g(V − E_K) is zero when V = (E_Na + E_K)/2 = (+60 + (−90))/2 = −15 mV; the end-plate depolarises from −80 mV towards this reversal potential, which lies between the two single-ion equilibrium potentials.

subtopic: Chloroplast structure and the chemiosmotic mechanism: an artificial transmembrane proton gradient drives ATP synthesis in the dark (acid–base experiment)
learningObjective: Reason from an experiment that a transmembrane proton gradient (lumen acidic relative to stroma) is itself sufficient to drive photophosphorylation, distinguishing the chemiosmotic step from the light and electron-transport steps.
stem: Isolated thylakoids are kept in complete darkness throughout the following procedure. They are first soaked in a buffer at pH 4 until their interior (the thylakoid lumen) has equilibrated to pH 4. They are then transferred rapidly into a buffer at pH 8 that also contains ADP and inorganic phosphate. A brief burst of ATP synthesis is observed, even though no light is supplied and no electron donor or acceptor is added. Which conclusion is best supported by this result?
choices: A proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane, with the lumen acidic relative to the stroma, is by itself sufficient to drive ATP synthesis.
ATP synthesis in chloroplasts requires the photochemical excitation of chlorophyll, so the observed ATP must be an experimental artefact.
The ATP was generated by cyclic electron flow around photosystem I that was triggered by the sudden change in pH.
ATP was synthesised because protons were driven from the stroma into the lumen, further acidifying the interior.
The low external pH caused chlorophyll to release a photon internally, and this light-like event powered the ATP synthase.
explanation: This is the logic of the classic acid–base (acid-bath) experiment. Loading the lumen to pH 4 and then jumping the outside to pH 8 creates an artificial proton gradient (high H+ inside, low H+ outside) identical in polarity to the one the light reactions normally build. Protons flow out through ATP synthase, and the free energy of this movement phosphorylates ADP. Because ATP is made in darkness, with no electron transport, the experiment isolates the chemiosmotic step and shows that the proton-motive force alone is sufficient: light and electron transport are needed only to establish the gradient, not for the phosphorylation itself.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: The imposed gradient (lumen pH 4, stroma side pH 8) has the same polarity as the physiological one; protons exiting the lumen through ATP synthase carry enough free energy to make ATP with no light and no electron flow, confirming Mitchell's chemiosmotic mechanism.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: Assumes the phosphorylation step itself needs the photochemical excitation of chlorophyll. The experiment shows the opposite — light is required only to build the proton gradient, and once a gradient exists ATP synthesis proceeds in the dark. (Misconception: treating light as directly required for ATP synthase rather than for gradient formation.)
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: Attributes the ATP to cyclic electron flow. No electron transport can occur here: there is no light to excite the photosystems and no added electron donor or acceptor. The sole driving force is the pre-formed proton gradient. (Misconception: conflating the electron-transport chain with the separate ATP-synthase step.)
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: Reverses the proton direction. Protons flow from the acidic lumen (pH 4) to the alkaline exterior (pH 8) through ATP synthase, and this outward flow drives synthesis; the enzyme is not hydrolysing ATP to pump protons inward. (Misconception: confusing the ATP-synthesising mode with the reverse proton-pumping/ATP-hydrolysing mode.)
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: Invents an internal photon release by chlorophyll. There is no such phenomenon; the energy source is the electrochemical proton gradient, not any light-like event. (Misconception: the belief that some photon/light step must underlie any chloroplast ATP synthesis.)

subtopic: Light-dependent reactions: photon–electron–O2–NADPH stoichiometry of linear (non-cyclic) electron flow through two photosystems in series
learningObjective: Combine the photolysis stoichiometry of water with the two-photosystem (two-photon-per-electron) requirement and the two-electron nature of NADPH to quantify photons and NADPH per molecule of O2 released.
stem: In non-cyclic (linear) electron flow, electrons released by the photolysis of water pass in series through photosystem II and then photosystem I before reducing NADP+. Assume that each electron must absorb the energy of exactly one photon at each of the two photosystems. For a chloroplast to release one molecule of O2, how many photons must be absorbed in total, and how many molecules of NADPH are produced at the same time?
choices: 4 photons and 2 molecules of NADPH
8 photons and 4 molecules of NADPH
2 photons and 1 molecule of NADPH
4 photons and 4 molecules of NADPH
8 photons and 2 molecules of NADPH
explanation: Releasing one O2 requires oxidising two water molecules: 2 H2O → O2 + 4 H+ + 4 e−, giving four electrons. In linear flow each electron is energised twice — once at photosystem II and once at photosystem I — so 4 electrons × 2 photosystems = 8 photons. NADPH is a two-electron carrier (NADP+ + 2 e− + H+ → NADPH), so 4 electrons reduce only 2 NADP+, producing 2 NADPH. Hence 8 photons and 2 NADPH.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: The NADPH figure (2) is right, but 4 photons counts only one photon per electron, ignoring that each electron is re-energised by a second photon at photosystem I. Two photosystems in series demand 2 photons per electron. (Misconception: single-photosystem / one-photon-per-electron.)
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: The photon count (8) is correct, but this treats each electron as reducing one NADP+. Because NADPH accepts two electrons, four electrons make only 2 NADPH, not 4. (Misconception: NADPH as a one-electron carrier.)
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: Works on a per-electron basis rather than per O2. Producing one O2 requires oxidising two water molecules and moving four electrons, not one. (Misconception: O2 derived from a single water molecule/electron.)
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: Combines two errors — one photon per electron (ignoring PSI) and one NADPH per electron (ignoring that NADPH carries two electrons). Both the photon and NADPH counts are therefore too high/low respectively.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: Four electrons from two waters need 4 × 2 = 8 photons, and those four electrons reduce two NADP+ to give 2 NADPH.

subtopic: Cyclic versus non-cyclic photophosphorylation: cyclic electron flow around PSI balances the ATP:NADPH ratio demanded by the Calvin cycle
learningObjective: Integrate the fixed ATP:NADPH stoichiometry of the Calvin cycle with the outputs of linear versus cyclic electron flow to predict the metabolic consequence of losing cyclic flow.
stem: The Calvin cycle consumes ATP and NADPH in a fixed ratio of 3 ATP to 2 NADPH for every CO2 molecule fixed. Linear (non-cyclic) electron flow produces both coenzymes together, but in a ratio containing less than 3 ATP per 2 NADPH, whereas cyclic electron flow around photosystem I produces additional ATP and no NADPH. A mutant alga cannot carry out cyclic electron flow, although its linear electron flow is normal. Under conditions demanding maximal carbon fixation, what is the most likely consequence?
choices: NADPH tends to accumulate while ATP becomes limiting, so the rate of carbon fixation is restricted.
Carbon fixation is unaffected, because linear electron flow alone supplies ATP and NADPH in exactly the ratio the Calvin cycle requires.
Oxygen production stops, because cyclic electron flow is the source of the electrons used to reduce NADP+.
ATP tends to accumulate while NADPH becomes limiting, so the rate of carbon fixation is restricted.
The stroma becomes strongly acidic, because cyclic electron flow is the only process that moves protons into the thylakoid lumen.
explanation: Cyclic electron flow tops up ATP without making NADPH, letting the chloroplast raise its ATP:NADPH output to the 3:2 the Calvin cycle needs. Remove it and the only source of both coenzymes is linear flow, which delivers relatively too little ATP per NADPH. ATP therefore becomes the limiting reagent for CO2 fixation, while the NADPH that cannot be spent accumulates (the electron carriers become over-reduced). The rate of carbon fixation falls even though reducing power is abundant.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: Losing the ATP-only contribution of cyclic flow lowers the available ATP:NADPH ratio below the required 3:2, so ATP runs short and unused NADPH builds up, throttling carbon fixation.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: Assumes linear flow already meets the 3:2 demand. The stem states its ATP:NADPH ratio is below 3:2, which is precisely why cyclic flow is normally needed. (Misconception: that non-cyclic flow self-balances the Calvin cycle's coenzyme budget.)
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: The electrons that reduce NADP+ come from the photolysis of water via linear flow, not from cyclic flow. Cyclic flow neither splits water nor feeds NADP+, so O2 evolution continues. (Misconception: conflating cyclic flow with the water-splitting/NADP+-reducing linear pathway.)
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: Reverses which coenzyme is limiting. Cyclic flow supplies extra ATP, so its loss makes ATP scarce and NADPH plentiful, not the other way round. (Misconception: mixing up the outputs of cyclic flow.)
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: Linear electron flow also pumps protons into the lumen, so cyclic flow is not the only proton source; moreover losing a lumen-acidifying process would not acidify the stroma. (Misconception: attributing all proton pumping — and the wrong compartment — to cyclic flow.)

subtopic: Calvin cycle carbon bookkeeping: turns, CO2 fixed and G3P made per net triose exported, including RuBP regeneration
learningObjective: Track carbon atoms through the Calvin cycle to determine how many CO2 must be fixed and how many G3P are formed before regeneration to yield one net exported triose.
stem: In the Calvin cycle each turn fixes one molecule of CO2 onto one molecule of ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP). To release one net molecule of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P, a three-carbon sugar) from the cycle, several turns are needed, and most of the G3P produced must be used to regenerate RuBP. How many molecules of CO2 must be fixed, and how many molecules of G3P are produced in total, to yield one net exported G3P?
choices: 3 CO2 fixed and 6 G3P produced in total
1 CO2 fixed and 2 G3P produced in total
6 CO2 fixed and 12 G3P produced in total
3 CO2 fixed and 5 G3P produced in total
2 CO2 fixed and 4 G3P produced in total
explanation: Follow the carbon. Three turns fix three CO2 (3 carbons) onto three RuBP (3 × 5 = 15 carbons), giving 18 carbons total, which appear as six molecules of the three-carbon G3P (6 × 3 = 18). Of these six G3P, five (15 carbons) are consumed to regenerate the three RuBP, and the remaining one G3P (3 carbons) is the net product that leaves the cycle. Hence 3 CO2 fixed and 6 G3P produced in total for one net exported G3P.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: Three CO2 combine with three RuBP to give 18 carbons as six G3P; five G3P regenerate the RuBP and one G3P is the net export.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: Assumes one turn (one CO2) yields one exportable G3P directly. G3P has three carbons, so at least three CO2 are needed, and the regeneration of RuBP is ignored entirely. (Misconception: one CO2 → one usable sugar molecule.)
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: These are the figures for making one glucose (a six-carbon sugar, i.e. two exported G3P: 6 CO2, 12 G3P). The question asks for one net G3P, which needs half of that. (Misconception: conflating a hexose budget with a single triose.)
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: The number of CO2 (3) is correct, but 5 counts only the G3P recycled to regenerate RuBP and omits the sixth molecule that is exported. Six G3P are formed in total. (Misconception: equating total G3P produced with the number recycled.)
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: A carbon-counting error giving two CO2. Two fixed carbons cannot balance the three-carbon net product plus RuBP regeneration. (Misconception: mis-tallying carbons entering versus leaving.)

subtopic: Limiting factors and the photosynthesis–respiration relationship: gross versus net CO2 exchange and the light compensation point
learningObjective: Interpret CO2 gas-exchange data to separate gross photosynthesis from net exchange using a constant respiration rate, and correctly identify the light compensation point.
stem: A single leaf is enclosed in a sealed chamber and its CO2 exchange is measured. In complete darkness the leaf releases CO2 at 5 arbitrary units per hour. At a low light intensity L1 the net CO2 exchange of the leaf is exactly zero. At a higher light intensity L2 the leaf shows a net uptake of CO2 of 15 units per hour. Assuming respiration proceeds at the same rate in the light as in the dark, which statement is correct?
choices: The gross rate of photosynthesis at L2 is 10 units per hour, and L1 is the light saturation point.
The gross rate of photosynthesis at L2 is 20 units per hour, and L1 is the light compensation point, where gross photosynthesis equals respiration.
The gross rate of photosynthesis at L2 is 20 units per hour, and at L1 both photosynthesis and respiration have stopped.
The gross rate of photosynthesis at L2 is 5 units per hour, and L1 is the CO2 compensation point.
The gross rate of photosynthesis at L2 is 15 units per hour, and L1 is the intensity at which photosynthesis has stopped altogether.
explanation: The measured net CO2 uptake already has the leaf's own respiratory CO2 release subtracted from it, because both processes run simultaneously in the light. Gross (true) photosynthesis = net uptake + respiration = 15 + 5 = 20 units per hour at L2. At L1 the net exchange is zero, which means gross photosynthesis is exactly balancing respiration (both equal to 5 units per hour); this is the definition of the light compensation point. Respiration does not stop there — the two opposing fluxes simply cancel.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: Subtracts respiration from net uptake (15 − 5 = 10), the wrong operation, and mislabels L1 as the light saturation point, which is where extra light no longer raises the rate — not where net exchange is zero. (Misconception: treating respiration as a further sink and confusing compensation with saturation.)
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: Adding the ongoing respiration (5) to the net uptake (15) gives a gross photosynthetic rate of 20; zero net exchange at L1 means gross photosynthesis equals respiration, i.e. the light compensation point.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: The gross rate (20) is right, but respiration does not cease at L1. Net exchange is zero there because gross photosynthesis (5) exactly offsets continuing respiration (5). (Misconception: believing respiration switches off at the compensation point.)
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: Reports only the respiration rate (5) as gross photosynthesis and mislabels L1 as the CO2 compensation point, which concerns CO2 concentration, not light intensity. (Misconception: confusing the respiration rate with gross photosynthesis and confusing light with CO2 compensation.)
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: Takes the measured net uptake (15) as the gross rate, forgetting that respiration is running at the same time, and misreads zero net exchange at L1 as photosynthesis having stopped rather than balancing respiration. (Misconception: net exchange equals gross photosynthesis.)

subtopic: Restriction enzymes with compatible cohesive ends (BamHI/BglII): junction-site destruction and non-excisability of the insert
learningObjective: Predict the fate of a restriction site when fragments with compatible cohesive ends produced by two different enzymes are ligated, and its consequence for insert recovery.
stem: The restriction endonuclease BamHI recognises 5'-G^GATCC-3' and BglII recognises 5'-A^GATCT-3'; both cleave to leave identical 5'-GATC single-stranded overhangs, so a BamHI-cut end can be ligated to a BglII-cut end. A gene fragment excised with BglII is ligated into a plasmid vector that has been linearised at its single BamHI site, and a recombinant plasmid carrying one copy of the insert is recovered. Which statement about this recombinant is correct?
choices: The insert can be excised with BglII but not with BamHI, because only the BglII site survives.
Ligation could not have occurred, because BamHI and BglII recognise different sequences.
The insert can be released again by digestion with BamHI, which regenerates its original recognition site at each junction.
Neither BamHI nor BglII can excise the insert, because each junction is a hybrid sequence recognised by neither enzyme.
Only one insert-vector junction can form; the opposite end of the insert remains single-stranded.
explanation: Ligation is governed by overhang complementarity, not by identity of the recognition sequence: BamHI and BglII both leave a 5'-GATC overhang, so their ends anneal and ligate. However, the recognition sequences differ in the flanking base. Joining a BamHI end (G side) to a BglII end regenerates the top strand G+GATC+T = GGATCT, and the reciprocal junction reads AGATCC. Neither GGATCT nor AGATCC is a BamHI site (GGATCC) or a BglII site (AGATCT). Both vector-insert junctions are therefore hybrids that neither enzyme can re-cleave, so the insert cannot be excised with BamHI or BglII (a different enzyme, or one recognising GATC such as Sau3AI, would be needed).

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: both junctions are BamHI/BglII hybrids and both are destroyed, so no BglII site survives either; the supposed asymmetry does not exist. Misconception: that one of the two parental sites is selectively preserved.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: ligation depends on complementary single-stranded overhangs, not on identical recognition sequences; both enzymes leave a GATC overhang, so the ends ligate readily. Misconception: equating recognition-site identity with ligation compatibility.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: joining a BamHI G-end to a BglII end yields a hybrid junction (GGATCT/AGATCC) that is neither a BamHI nor a BglII site, so BamHI cannot regenerate or cut it. Misconception: assuming compatible overhangs restore the original recognition site.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: both junctions are hybrid sequences (GGATCT and AGATCC) recognised by neither BamHI nor BglII, so the insert cannot be excised by either enzyme.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: to form a circular recombinant plasmid the insert must join the vector at BOTH of its ends, creating two junctions; a molecule left single-stranded at one end could not circularise. Misconception: that only one cohesive end participates.

subtopic: Bacteriophage one-step growth: burst size per infected cell at low multiplicity of infection
learningObjective: Calculate bacteriophage burst size from one-step growth data, distinguishing the number of infected cells from the total cell count.
stem: In a one-step growth experiment, 5 x 10^8 sensitive bacteria are mixed with 1 x 10^7 particles of a virulent bacteriophage. Adsorption is essentially complete, and the low phage-to-cell ratio makes it very unlikely that any cell is infected by more than one phage. Unadsorbed phage are washed away. After one synchronous round of intracellular replication, all infected cells lyse and the total phage titre reaches 8 x 10^8. What is the average burst size (progeny particles released per infected cell)?
explanation: Burst size is the number of progeny phage released divided by the number of cells that actually became infected. With a multiplicity of infection of 1 x 10^7 / 5 x 10^8 = 0.02, essentially every adsorbed phage enters a separate cell, so the number of infected cells equals the number of adsorbed phage, 1 x 10^7. The infecting phage are in the eclipse phase inside the cells (no free phage remain after washing), so the 8 x 10^8 particles after lysis are all progeny. Burst size = 8 x 10^8 / 1 x 10^7 = 80.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: divides the progeny by the TOTAL number of bacteria (8 x 10^8 / 5 x 10^8 = 1.6), ignoring that only 1 x 10^7 of the cells were actually infected. Misconception: treating every bacterium as a phage producer.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: subtracts the 1 x 10^7 input phage from the progeny first, (8 x 10^8 - 1 x 10^7)/1 x 10^7 = 79. The infecting phage are eclipsed inside the cells, not free particles to be subtracted. Misconception: double-counting the input as surviving free phage.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: only the 1 x 10^7 adsorbed phage establish infections (MOI ~0.02, at most one per cell), so 8 x 10^8 progeny / 1 x 10^7 infected cells = 80.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: divides the bacteria by the phage (5 x 10^8 / 1 x 10^7 = 50), swapping the roles of the two counts. Misconception: confusing cell number with progeny number.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: simply reads off the coefficient of the final titre (8 x 10^8) and ignores the number of infected cells entirely. Misconception: mistaking the mantissa of the titre for the burst size.

subtopic: PCR product length: locating primer binding sites and adding a non-annealing 5' tail
learningObjective: Determine the length of a PCR amplicon from primer binding positions, correctly including a non-templated 5' primer tail.
stem:
A linear DNA template is numbered 1-1000 along the top strand (5'->3'). A PCR is set up with two primers:
- Forward primer: 20 nucleotides, perfectly matching the top-strand sequence at positions 201-220 (its 5' end at position 201).
- Reverse primer: 24 nucleotides. Its 3'-terminal 18 nucleotides are complementary to the top strand at positions 480-497; its remaining 5' 6 nucleotides are an added restriction-site 'tail' that does not match the template.
After many cycles, what is the length of the predominant double-stranded product?
choices: 297 bp
286 bp
309 bp
303 bp
296 bp
explanation: The final amplicon runs from the 5' end of the forward primer to the 5' end of the reverse primer, and it incorporates any non-templated 5' tails. The forward primer's 5' end sits at position 201. The reverse primer's 18 template-matching nucleotides cover positions 480-497, so its 5' end corresponds to position 497 (497 - 480 + 1 = 18). The template-defined core therefore spans 201 to 497 = 497 - 201 + 1 = 297 bp. The reverse primer adds a 6-nucleotide tail that is copied into the product from the second cycle onward, while the forward primer has no tail. Total product length = 297 + 6 = 303 bp.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 497 - 201 + 1 = 297 correctly counts the template-defined core but omits the 6-nt non-annealing tail, which becomes part of the amplicon. Misconception: that only template-matching bases contribute to product length.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: measures to the reverse primer's 3' end (position 480) instead of its 5' end (position 497): 480 - 201 + 1 = 280, plus the 6-nt tail = 286. The amplicon extends to the 5' end of each primer, not the 3' end. Misconception: taking the 3' (extension) end as the amplicon boundary.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: adds a 6-nt tail at BOTH ends (297 + 6 + 6 = 309), but only the reverse primer carries a tail; the forward primer matches the template exactly. Misconception: assuming both primers add tails.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: core span 201-497 = 297 bp plus the 6-nt reverse-primer tail = 303 bp.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 497 - 201 = 296 makes an off-by-one error (failing to count both endpoints inclusively) and also omits the 6-nt tail. Two errors that partially cancel toward a plausible value.

subtopic: Agarose gel electrophoresis of plasmid DNA: conformation-dependent migration (supercoiled vs linear vs open-circular) using nicking and single-cut controls
learningObjective: Interpret the multiple bands of an undigested plasmid preparation as supercoiled, linear and open-circular conformations using nicking and single-cut controls.
stem: A preparation of a single, intact double-stranded circular plasmid (all molecules identical in length) is electrophoresed on an agarose gel and gives three bands: band 1 (fastest-migrating), band 2 (intermediate) and band 3 (slowest). When a sample is first treated with a nicking enzyme that makes a single-strand break in every molecule (without cutting both strands or shortening the DNA), the whole sample runs as band 3. When a separate sample is treated with a restriction enzyme that cuts each molecule exactly once, the whole sample runs as band 2. Which interpretation of the three bands is correct?
choices: Band 3 is the supercoiled form, because supercoiled DNA is the most compact and therefore migrates most slowly.

Band 1 is supercoiled, band 2 is full-length linear and band 3 is the open-circular (relaxed) form; a single nick relaxes the supercoils (band 1 -> band 3) and a single double-strand cut linearises the molecule (-> band 2).
Band 2 is open-circular and band 3 is linear; the linear form runs slowest because cutting the plasmid makes it longer.
The three bands are the same conformation but three different lengths; the preparation is contaminated with two additional plasmids.
Band 1 is open-circular, band 2 is supercoiled and band 3 is linear.
explanation: For DNA of a single length, migration through agarose depends on conformation. The controls fix the identities directly: a single-strand nick relaxes supercoiled DNA to the open-circular form, and that product is band 3 (the slowest), so band 3 = open-circular. A single double-strand cut converts the circle to a full-length linear molecule, and that product is band 2 (intermediate), so band 2 = linear. The remaining band 1 (fastest) must be the compact supercoiled form. Thus identical-length molecules migrate at supercoiled > linear > open-circular, and the data force this assignment regardless of any memorised ordering.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: supercoiling makes the molecule more compact, so it migrates FASTER, not slower; the data also show the slowest band is the nicking (open-circular) product. Misconception: 'more compact means slower migration.'
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: nicking (which yields open-circular DNA) gives band 3, so band 3 is open-circular; a single cut (which yields linear DNA) gives band 2, so band 2 is linear; the remaining fastest band 1 is supercoiled. Conformation, not length, sets the migration order.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: the single-cut (linear) product is band 2, not band 3, and cutting a circle does not change its contour length; the migration differences are due to conformation, not length. Misconception: that linearising a circle lengthens the DNA.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: the treatments interconvert the bands (nicking -> band 3, single cut -> band 2), proving all three are conformations of one molecule rather than three different plasmids. Misconception: that every gel band must correspond to a different length.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: it assigns the fastest band to the open-circular form, but the nicking treatment (which produces open-circular DNA) gives the SLOWEST band. Misconception: that the relaxed circle is the most compact and therefore fastest.

subtopic: Restriction digestion of a circular plasmid with two enzymes: counting the fragments produced
learningObjective: Apply the rule that a fully digested circular DNA molecule yields as many fragments as there are cut sites, and combine the sites of two enzymes.
stem: A circular bacterial plasmid contains three recognition sites for the restriction enzyme EcoRI and two recognition sites for the restriction enzyme BamHI; all five sites lie at different positions around the plasmid. If a sample of the plasmid is completely digested with BOTH enzymes together, how many linear DNA fragments are produced?
explanation: Each cut in a closed circular molecule that is already open contributes one extra fragment, but the first cut merely opens the circle into one linear piece; overall a circular molecule cut at n distinct sites is divided into exactly n fragments (not n + 1, which is the rule for a linear molecule). Here the two enzymes together cut at 3 + 2 = 5 distinct sites, so a complete double digest gives 5 fragments.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 3 counts only the EcoRI sites and ignores the two BamHI sites present in the same double digest.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 4 counts only... it undercounts the sites; there are five distinct cut sites (three + two), and a circular molecule gives one fragment per site.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 6 applies the linear-molecule rule (n + 1 fragments); a circle has no free ends, so n cuts give n fragments, i.e. 5, not 6.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 2 counts only the BamHI sites and ignores the three EcoRI sites.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: a circular molecule cut at n distinct sites yields n fragments; with 3 + 2 = 5 sites the double digest produces 5 fragments.

subtopic: Mechanics of ventilation: intrapleural pressure, opposing elastic recoil and pneumothorax
learningObjective: Explain how the sub-atmospheric intrapleural pressure results from the opposing elastic recoil of the lung (inward) and chest wall (outward), and predict the mechanical consequence of opening the pleural space to the atmosphere.
stem: At rest between breaths (end-expiration), the pressure inside the pleural cavity is slightly below atmospheric pressure because the elastic recoil of the lungs pulls them inwards while the elastic recoil of the chest wall pulls it outwards. A patient sustains a stab wound that opens the pleural cavity on one side to the outside air (an open pneumothorax). Assuming no air is actively pumped in or out through the wound, which change is expected on the injured side?
choices: Neither the lung nor the chest wall changes shape, because their pressures were already balanced.
Both the lung and the chest wall collapse inwards together.
Both the lung and the chest wall spring outwards and enlarge.
The lung expands further outwards while the chest wall is drawn inwards.
The lung recoils and collapses inwards while the chest wall springs outwards.
explanation: Between breaths the lung is held stretched against its own inward elastic recoil only because the intrapleural pressure is sub-atmospheric, creating a positive transpulmonary pressure (alveolar minus intrapleural) that keeps the alveoli open. This sub-atmospheric pressure exists because the inward pull of the lung and the outward pull of the (larger-at-rest) chest wall act against each other across the sealed pleural space. When the pleural cavity is opened to the atmosphere, air enters until intrapleural pressure equals atmospheric pressure. The transpulmonary gradient is abolished, so the lung is no longer held expanded and collapses under its own inward recoil, while the chest wall, released from the lung's inward pull, springs outwards toward its own larger resting volume (the classic barrel-out of the chest with lung collapse).

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: assumes opening the pleura changes nothing because the system was 'balanced'. The balance depended on the sealed, sub-atmospheric pleural space; removing that seal is precisely what changes the geometry.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: treats the chest-wall recoil as inward. In fact the relaxed chest wall's equilibrium (resting) volume is larger than the functional residual capacity, so it recoils OUTWARD, not inward.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: assumes the lung, like the chest wall, springs outward. This misconception ignores that lung elastic tissue and surface tension produce a net INWARD recoil; only the chest wall recoils outward.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: reverses both recoil tendencies — it assumes the lung intrinsically tends to expand and the chest wall to collapse. In reality the lung's elastic recoil is inward (it tends to collapse) and the relaxed chest wall's recoil is outward.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: losing the seal raises intrapleural pressure to atmospheric, abolishing the transpulmonary pressure that held the lung open. The lung collapses inward under its own recoil while the chest wall expands outward toward its resting volume.

subtopic: Carbon-dioxide transport as hydrogencarbonate: the reverse chloride shift in the pulmonary capillaries
learningObjective: Trace the fate of hydrogencarbonate and chloride ions across the red-cell membrane as blood is oxygenated in the lung, recognising that the tissue-level chloride shift reverses so that CO2 can be regenerated intracellularly and exhaled.
stem: Most carbon dioxide is carried in the blood as hydrogencarbonate (bicarbonate) ions dissolved in the plasma. This bicarbonate is generated inside red blood cells by carbonic anhydrase and is then exported into the plasma. Consider a single red blood cell as it passes through a pulmonary (lung) capillary and gives up carbon dioxide to the alveolar air. Which combination of events best describes what happens at that red cell during this passage?
choices: Hydrogencarbonate ions and chloride ions both enter the red cell, together raising its internal solute content.
No net ion movement occurs; the plasma hydrogencarbonate is converted to carbon dioxide directly in the plasma and exhaled without re-entering the red cell.
Chloride ions enter the red cell and hydrogencarbonate ions leave it, while inside the cell carbon dioxide is converted into still more hydrogencarbonate.
Chloride ions leave the red cell and hydrogencarbonate ions enter it, and inside the cell hydrogencarbonate combines with H+ to reform carbon dioxide, which then diffuses out.
Hydrogencarbonate ions and chloride ions both leave the red cell, so that the cell loses solute and shrinks.
explanation: In the tissues the 'forward' chloride shift occurs: CO2 enters the red cell, carbonic anhydrase forms carbonic acid which dissociates to H+ and HCO3-, and HCO3- is exported to the plasma in exchange for Cl- entering the cell (electroneutral antiport). In the lung every step runs in reverse. To exhale CO2, the plasma bicarbonate must be reconverted to CO2, but carbonic anhydrase is inside the red cell, so HCO3- must re-enter the cell. It does so in exchange for Cl- moving out (the reverse chloride shift). Inside the cell, HCO3- combines with H+ (released as haemoglobin becomes oxygenated — the Haldane effect) to form carbonic acid, which carbonic anhydrase converts to CO2 and water; the CO2 then diffuses out to the alveolus. Thus in the lungs the red cell's chloride content falls as bicarbonate enters.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: has both anions entering at once. The transport is an electroneutral antiport (one anion in for one anion out); both cannot enter without an equal counter-movement, so this violates the exchange mechanism.
